title: Repair a snapped barbed-wire strand without a fence stretcher
mechanism_check: Wire holds by tension between two fixed posts; a broken strand sags because the tension path is severed, not because the wire is weak.
Staples pin wire to posts but carry no tension — the splice must rebuild the tension line end-to-end.
Barbed wire under load stores energy: it recoils toward the nearest anchor when cut, which is what makes a loose cut dangerous.
improvised_tools: Two locking pliers or vise-grips (one per side of the break) as hand-pullers
A length of scrap wire as a pull-loop or Spanish windlass
Pliers or a multi-tool for twisting the splice
A stick or hammer handle to lever extra pull distance
steps: Locate both broken ends; keep clear of the recoil side until ends are secured to their nearest posts.
Wrap each broken end with locking pliers, leaving 12 inches of free wire past each jaw.
Hook a scrap-wire loop between the two pliers and twist it with a stick as a windlass until the two broken ends overlap by 6-8 inches.
Twist the two wire ends together with pliers: three tight wraps each direction, no sharp stubs left sticking out.
Release the windlass tension slowly; confirm the splice sits inside the fence line, not bowing outward.
Walk 50 feet either direction and re-staple any wire the shock wave shook loose.
stop_conditions: STOP if the broken end is buried under a fallen tree or entangled with a downed power line — call the utility, do not cut or pull.
STOP if you cannot get overlap: the break is too far from a post — splice in a new section of wire instead.
STOP if the wire frays and snaps twice in a row: the whole strand is corroded and must be replaced, not spliced.
STOP if livestock are pressing the fence while you work — move animals off the line before touching wire under tension.

title: Build a temporary electric-fence corner post from a cut limb
mechanism_check: An electric corner post only has to hold insulators at the right height and resist the sideways pull of the tape or wire turning the corner.
Sideways pull is the failure mode: a plain driven stake tips toward the fence; a braced or footed post resists it.
Insulators must keep live wire off the post — wet wood conducts enough to bleed the charge.
improvised_tools: A straight 5-6 foot hardwood limb, 3-4 inches thick, as the post
A shorter limb driven at an angle as a brace
Screw-in or nail-on insulators; in a pinch, split garden hose sections as standoff sleeves
Rocks or a shovel for tamping the post hole
steps: Cut the limb and strip bark where insulators will mount — bark traps moisture and bleeds voltage.
Drive the post 18 inches deep at the corner, leaning slightly away from the fence pull direction.
Drive the brace limb at 45 degrees against the post on the inside of the corner, 12 inches deep.
Mount insulators or hose-sleeve standoffs at fence height before stringing wire — retrofitting them under a live wire is asking for a shock.
String the corner, then tension the fence wire; the post should not shift.
Re-tamp the soil after the first rain, when the disturbed ground settles.
stop_conditions: STOP if the post shifts under load: dig deeper or add a second brace rather than stacking more tension on a weak post.
STOP if the fence energizer is unknown or untested — verify the unit is rated for livestock before turning animals out on the line.
STOP if you have no insulators and no hose sleeve: a live wire on bare wood will bleed out and the fence will fail.
STOP if children or pets treat the fence as a toy — post a barrier and a warning sign before energizing.

title: Improvise a gate hinge from scrap metal and a bolt
mechanism_check: A gate hinge has two jobs: a fixed pin carries the shear load and a leaf plate spreads that load into the post so lag screws do not tear out.
Sagging gates fail at the plate-to-post interface, not at the pin — undersized plates on soft wood are the usual cause.
The pin must allow vertical lift-off so the gate can be removed; a captured pin that cannot be lifted traps the gate on the post.
improvised_tools: A 3/8-inch or larger bolt with nut as the hinge pin
Flat scrap steel (mower blade, angle iron, flat bar) for the leaf plates
Drill or a heated punch for bolt holes
Lag screws or carriage bolts to mount plates
steps: Cut two leaf plates at least 6 inches long and 2 inches wide; drill a pin hole near one end of each.
Mount one plate horizontally on the post and one on the gate stile, aligned so the pin holes sit on the same vertical line.
Drop the bolt through both holes as the pin; thread the nut on loosely, not tight — the nut must keep the pin captive without binding rotation.
Grease or oil the pin; swing the gate through its full arc and watch for plate flex.
If the post flexes, sister a second plate or move the hinge to a taller, sound post before the screws pull out.
For a lift-off gate, leave the top pin plate slotted or un-nutted so the gate lifts off when raised.
stop_conditions: STOP if the post is rotted at hinge height: no plate fixes bad wood — set a new post first.
STOP if the bolt is under 3/8 inch for a stock gate: a shear pin this small will bend and drop the gate on an animal.
STOP if the gate swings toward livestock pens or a road and cannot be latched — do not finish until the latch side is secured.
STOP if you are drilling or grinding near dry bedding or grass — move the work to bare ground and keep water handy.

title: Patch a leaking galvanized stock tank with a bolted rubber patch
mechanism_check: Water finds the path of least resistance: a pinhole leak is sealed only if the patch clamps the metal flat around the hole — sealant alone creeps under water pressure.
Galvanized steel flexes with water weight; a rigid-only patch cracks at its edges, so the patch must compress a gasket as the tank breathes.
The seal surface must be clean bare metal; rust scale and algae under a patch are a guaranteed second leak.
improvised_tools: A scrap of inner tube or EPDM as gasket material
A rigid backing plate (plywood scrap, flat steel, even a license plate)
Bolts with fender washers and nuts; silicone or roof cement as bed sealant
Wire brush, sandpaper, or a rock for scouring the rust off
steps: Drain the tank below the leak and let the metal dry; mark the leak with chalk.
Scour the area to bare bright metal for 3 inches in every direction past the hole.
Cut the rubber gasket 2 inches larger than the hole and the backing plate the same size.
Bed the gasket in silicone, sandwich rubber between tank and backing plate, and bolt through with fender washers on both sides.
Tighten in a star pattern until sealant squeezes out evenly around the plate — this is the compression doing the sealing.
Refill and watch for weeping at the plate edge for 24 hours before letting animals drink.
stop_conditions: STOP if the leak is at a seam that is splitting along its length: a patch will not hold a structural failure — the tank needs a new panel or replacement.
STOP if rust has perforated a large area: patching lace will just move the leak sideways.
STOP if you must use sealants with unknown toxicity: use only food/water-safe silicone on a drinking-water tank.
STOP if the tank wall flexes so much the plate cannot sit flat: drain fully, brace the wall, then patch.

title: Replace a broken tool handle with a carved greenwood branch
mechanism_check: A handle transmits striking force through the head socket; the wood must fill the socket completely or the head loosens on every swing.
Greenwood shrinks as it dries, so an oversized green handle will shrink INTO the socket and lock tighter — carve it fat, not thin.
The weak axis is the head-to-eye fit, not the grip length: 1/8 inch of slop at the eye becomes inches of wobble at the head.
improvised_tools: A straight hardwood branch (hickory, oak, ash) slightly thicker than the socket
A hatchet or knife for shaping
Sandpaper or a smooth stone to ease the grip
A wooden wedge and a steel wedge (or a nail cluster) for the eye
steps: Split or saw the branch a few inches longer than the old handle; leave the bark on the grip section.
Shape the head end with a hatchet to a snug taper that starts entering the socket with hand pressure only.
Drive the handle through the socket until 1 inch protrudes; trim the excess.
Cut a kerf across the protruding end, drive a wooden wedge in with the grain, then seat a steel wedge crosswise to lock it.
Let the handle dry a week before heavy use; re-check the eye after the first day of work.
Oil the grip or wrap it with tape where blisters form.
stop_conditions: STOP if the head itself is cracked at the eye: a new handle on a cracked head is a projectile waiting to happen.
STOP if the only available branch is soft wood (pine, willow) for a striking tool: use it for a rake, not a sledge.
STOP if the branch is dead and punky: it will snap on the first swing — test by flexing hard before carving.
STOP if the wedge kerf splits the handle end: shave it back and re-cut, do not drive a wedge into a split.

title: Build a gravity-fed drip irrigation line from a raised barrel
mechanism_check: Gravity systems run on head pressure: every 2.3 feet of elevation gives roughly 1 psi, and drip emitters need a steady minimum to flow evenly.
The failure mode is uneven flow — high rows flood while low rows starve — so elevation must be measured from the barrel bottom to the lowest row, not the top.
A barrel at rest grows algae and sediment; unfiltered water plugs emitters from the inside, which is invisible until the row is dead.
improvised_tools: A 55-gallon barrel or tote on blocks, stand, or a hillside as the reservoir
Garden hose or poly tubing for the main line
Emitters improvised from nail-pierced tubing, or bought drip emitters
A sock, screen, or cloth filter at the barrel outlet
steps: Raise the barrel so its bottom is at least 4 feet above the highest garden row; more elevation is better.
Plumb the outlet from the SIDE of the barrel, 3 inches above the bottom, so sediment settles below the draw point.
Fit a simple filter (cloth bag, window screen) over the outlet inside the barrel.
Run the main line level along the top of the rows; punch emitter holes pointing down, smaller than you think — you can always enlarge.
Flush the line with emitters open before capping ends; sediment left in the line becomes clogs.
Cover the barrel against light to stop algae; scrub the filter weekly during the growing season.
stop_conditions: STOP if the barrel cannot be made stable at height: 55 gallons weighs 450 pounds — a collapsing stand is a crushing hazard.
STOP if elevation is under 3 feet above the highest row: the line will not run evenly — switch to a siphon or hand-watering instead.
STOP if the water source is treated runoff of unknown chemistry: test it before putting it on food crops.
STOP if you cannot keep the barrel covered: open standing water breeds mosquitoes.

title: Build a rainwater catchment from a roof gutter and totes
mechanism_check: A roof is a funnel: 1 inch of rain on 1,000 square feet yields about 600 gallons, so storage size — not collection — is the real constraint.
The first flush carries roof grime, bird droppings, and grit; diverting the first few gallons away from storage is what makes the water usable.
Overflow is the silent killer: a full tote in a downpour sends hundreds of gallons against a foundation if the overflow has no plan.
improvised_tools: Gutter sections and a downspout, new or salvaged
Food-grade totes (IBC) or barrels as storage
A 5-gallon bucket as a first-flush diverter
Screen mesh for the inlet and a spigot for draw-off
steps: Hang the gutter with a slight fall (1/4 inch per 10 feet) toward the downspout end; level gutters pond and breed mosquitoes.
Run the downspout into the first-flush bucket with a slow-drain hole: the bucket fills with the dirtiest water, then a standpipe routes cleaner water to the totes.
Link totes in series from the top so they fill evenly, and put the draw-off spigot at the lowest tote.
Screen every inlet against mosquitoes and debris; seal tote lids but leave a vent.
Route the overflow pipe at least 10 feet away from any foundation, downhill.
Label non-potable unless filtered and tested — do not plumb it into the house without a proper treatment setup.
stop_conditions: STOP if the roof has asbestos, lead paint, or fresh tar: the water is not safe to catch.
STOP if totes cannot be secured against wind: a full IBC weighs a ton; an empty one sails.
STOP if the structure cannot hold the weight: water is 8.3 pounds per gallon — a 275-gallon tote is over a ton.
STOP if freezing weather is coming and totes are full: drain them or accept burst seams.

title: Build a three-bin compost system from shipping pallets
mechanism_check: Compost needs air, moisture, and a carbon-nitrogen mix; a single pile fails because turning it means lifting the whole mass — bins let you fork material forward, not upward.
Three bins run a pipeline: fresh, cooking, finished. Two bins always leave you with nowhere to turn the active pile.
Pallet slats give airflow by accident of design — the gaps are the aeration system.
improvised_tools: Nine to twelve wooden pallets, heat-treated (HT stamp) not fumigated
A sledgehammer and scrap 2x4s for driving stakes
T-posts or stakes to anchor the pallet walls
A pitchfork for turning
steps: Pick a shaded, well-drained spot you can reach with a wheelbarrow year-round.
Stand pallets on edge to form three side-by-side bins, roughly 3x3 feet each; anchor corners with driven stakes.
Leave the front open or hinged with wire loops so you can fork material out.
Fill bin one with a 3:1 mix of browns (leaves, straw, cardboard) to greens (scraps, manure, grass).
When bin one is full and heating, fork it into bin two — that turn IS the aeration the pile needs.
Bin two cooks while bin three holds finished compost; harvest bin three and the cycle rotates.
stop_conditions: STOP if pallets are marked MB (methyl bromide fumigated): do not compost in them or grow food near them.
STOP if you add meat, dairy, or pet waste: the pile will not get hot enough in a pallet bin to kill pathogens.
STOP if the pile smells like rot instead of earth: it is too wet or too nitrogen-heavy — add browns and turn it.
STOP if rodents move in: bury food scraps 12 inches deep or switch to a closed bin for kitchen waste.

title: Predator-proof a chicken coop with a hardware-cloth apron
mechanism_check: Predators do not break walls — they dig. Raccoons, foxes, and dogs go UNDER the edge of a coop, not through it.
A buried wire apron works because diggers start at the wall and dig straight down; they hit the apron and give up, lacking the sense to back up and tunnel wider.
Chicken wire stops chickens, not predators: its thin twists pull apart in raccoon hands. Hardware cloth (welded 1/2-inch) is the actual barrier.
improvised_tools: 1/2-inch hardware cloth, 2-3 feet wide, for the apron
Staples, screws with washers, or fence staples to attach it to the coop base
A shovel or sod cutter for a shallow trench
Rocks, pavers, or sod pins to pin the apron flat
steps: Dig a 6-inch trench around the entire coop perimeter, coop included — any gap is the gap they will find.
Staple or screw the hardware cloth to the coop base with washers every 6 inches; the attachment is the weak point, not the cloth.
Lay the cloth flat outward in the trench, extending 18-24 inches from the wall, and pin it down so it cannot be lifted.
Backfill the trench and pack it; grass will grow through and hide the apron within a season.
Check the apron after heavy rain exposes it, and re-bury promptly.
Lock the pop door at dusk every night — an apron does not stop a predator that walks through an open door.
stop_conditions: STOP if the coop sits on a slope where runoff will undercut the apron: regrade or extend the apron on the downhill side.
STOP if you find a predator already inside: clear the coop before sealing it, or you lock the problem in.
STOP if hardware cloth is unavailable and only chicken wire is on hand: delay the birds' move-in until real cloth is bought — wire is false security.
STOP if neighbors' dogs roam loose: an apron stops digging, not a determined dog hitting the wall — add a hot wire at nose height.

title: Sharpen a mower blade with a hand file when no grinder is available
mechanism_check: A mower blade cuts by speed, not razor sharpness: it needs the correct bevel angle and BALANCE, not a knife edge.
An unbalanced blade vibrates, and vibration is what destroys spindle bearings — a sharpened-but-unbalanced blade is worse than a dull balanced one.
The bevel goes on the TOP edge only; filing the flat underside changes the cutting geometry and lift.
improvised_tools: A flat bastard file or mill file (not a rasp)
A vise, C-clamp, or the mower deck itself as a holder
A nail through a board as a balance pivot
Motor oil or a rag to wipe the finished edge
steps: Disconnect the spark plug wire or unplug the battery before touching the blade — non-negotiable.
Remove the blade and clamp it flat-side-down; file the existing bevel, pushing the file away from your body, 10-15 strokes per side.
Restore the factory bevel angle; never grind a second bevel or thin the edge to a knife point.
Hang the blade on the nail pivot: if one side drops, file a few strokes off the heavy side until it sits level.
Reinstall with the lift wings pointing UP toward the deck and torque the bolt to spec.
Test-cut a patch of grass: even tearing, not shredding, is the sign you got it right.
stop_conditions: STOP if the blade is cracked, bent, or worn thin at the lift wings: sharpening a damaged blade makes a projectile — replace it.
STOP if you cannot get the blade balanced after several tries: take it to a shop for grinding rather than running it unbalanced.
STOP if the mounting bolt is damaged or the spindle wobbles: fix the mount before the blade.
STOP if the engine starts while your hands are near the blade: keep the plug wire off and grounded until reassembly is complete.

title: Set a t-post straight without a post driver
mechanism_check: A t-post holds by soil friction along its buried length, not by the hole: disturbed soil around a post is why hand-set posts lean.
The anchor plate (spade) near the post bottom is the anti-pullout mechanism — it must end up BELOW undisturbed soil level.
Straight matters more than deep for fence line wire tension: a leaning post shifts the whole wire plane.
improvised_tools: A heavy pipe, sledgehammer, or a section of thick-walled tubing slipped over the post as a driver
A shovel for a pilot hole in rocky ground
A level, or a plumb line made from string and a rock
A tamping bar or broom handle to pack the soil
steps: Mark the line with string first; every post location is decided before any driving starts.
In hard ground, dig a 6-inch pilot hole; in soft ground, drive directly.
Set the post with the studs (bumps) facing the direction the wire will be pulled from.
Drive to the post's painted depth line — usually 18-24 inches — checking plumb on two axes every few blows.
Tamp the soil hard around the base with the tamping bar; loose backfill is a leaning post by spring.
Attach wire only after the post is plumb and solid: never use the wire itself to straighten a crooked post.
stop_conditions: STOP if you hit solid rock: drive a shorter post, relocate, or drill — mushrooming the post top ruins it and bounces the hammer.
STOP if the ground is saturated mud: the post will set crooked and sink — wait for it to drain.
STOP if overhead lines are within a post length: keep the post flat while positioning, never raise it vertical near wires.
STOP if the post mushrooms or splits under the driver: stop and switch to a pilot-hole method before it fails.

title: Splice a broken fence rail with a scarf joint and wire lashing
mechanism_check: A butt joint fails because end grain glues and nails poorly; a scarf joint overlaps long grain with long grain, which is where wood joints get their strength.
Wire lashing supplies the clamping force that nails used to provide — it works only if the joint faces mate flat before lashing.
The joint must sit near a post, not mid-span: mid-span splices flex and the lashing works loose.
improvised_tools: A saw or hatchet to cut the scarf angles
Fence wire, baling wire, or twine for lashing
Pliers to twist the lashing tight
A chisel or flat rock to clean the joint faces
steps: Cut back both broken ends to sound wood; rot in the joint guarantees a second failure.
Cut matching 6-8 inch scarf bevels (long tapers, not steep) on both ends so the faces mate flat.
Test-fit dry: the joint should sit straight with no rocking before any lashing goes on.
Bind the joint with 6-8 tight wraps of wire on each side of the center, twisting the ends down hard with pliers.
Slide the joint to the nearest post and fasten it to the post with nails, screws, or a wire loop.
Seal the top of the joint against standing water with anything handy — even a tin can lid nailed over it.
stop_conditions: STOP if the rail is rotted through beyond the joint area: splice only into sound wood.
STOP if the joint will carry stock pressure mid-span with no post nearby: set a new post instead.
STOP if the lashing wire keeps snapping: the joint faces are not mating flat — recut before re-lashing.
STOP if the fence line is electric: de-energize before cutting or handling wire near the circuit.

title: Build an emergency animal shelter lean-to from poles and tarps
mechanism_check: Animals die of wind and wet, not cold alone: the shelter's job is breaking wind and keeping bedding dry, not heating air.
A lean-to sheds weather one direction; orient the open side AWAY from prevailing storm winds or it becomes a wind tunnel.
Tarps fail at the tie points: every attachment spreads load or the tarp rips out in the first gust.
improvised_tools: Cut poles, salvaged lumber, or t-posts for the frame
Tarps, billboard vinyl, or feed sacks sewn together for the roof and back wall
Rope, baling twine, or wire for lashing
Straw, shavings, or dry leaves for bedding
steps: Site it on high, well-drained ground — a shelter in a puddle is a pneumonia box.
Set two tall back poles and two shorter front poles (or a fence line as the back) to make a single-slope frame.
Lash cross poles across the top; the roof plane must have no sag where water can pond.
Drape the tarp over the roof and down the back wall; wrap tarp edges around the poles and lash through the grommets with rope, not the bare grommet holes alone.
Bank straw bales or earth around the two sides to block cross-draft at animal height.
Bed deep with dry straw; plan to re-bed after every storm — wet bedding is the actual killer.
stop_conditions: STOP if the tarp cannot be lashed at every grommet: a loose tarp in a storm becomes a sail and can injure animals.
STOP if the only site is a low spot that floods: wait out the storm with animals in the barn instead.
STOP if poles are dead-rotted: test by bending hard before trusting them overhead.
STOP if you must shelter animals with horns in a low lean-to: raise the front to at least 6 feet so horns cannot snag the tarp and collapse it.

title: Thaw a frozen stock-tank water line safely with warm water and insulation
mechanism_check: Ice expands and splits pipes at the weakest fitting, not along straight runs: the freeze point is almost always at an elbow, valve, or exposed riser.
Pouring boiling water on a frozen metal pipe creates thermal shock that cracks fittings — gradual warmth is the mechanism, not brute heat.
The permanent fix is insulation and drainage AFTER the thaw, because the same spot will freeze again on the next cold night.
improvised_tools: Warm (not boiling) water in buckets or jugs
Towels, blankets, or feed sacks to hold heat against the pipe
A hair dryer or heat gun on low, if power is available — never an open flame
Pipe insulation, foam, or wrapped feed sacks for after the thaw
steps: Find the freeze point: feel along the line for the cold, hard section, usually at a fitting or where the line leaves the ground.
Wrap the frozen section in towels and pour warm water over the wrap repeatedly — the wrap holds heat against the pipe.
Open the downstream valve or tap so meltwater has somewhere to go; pressure behind the ice is what bursts fittings.
Once water flows, run it briefly to clear slush, then insulate the section: wrap with feed sacks or foam and tie securely.
Drain or bury the vulnerable section deeper before the next freeze; add a drain valve at the low point.
Check the tank heater and the line every morning in a cold snap — catch it before it freezes solid.
stop_conditions: STOP if the pipe is already split and spraying: shut off the supply and plan a repair, not a thaw.
STOP before using any torch or open flame on the line: it cracks fittings, melts plastic, and starts bedding fires.
STOP if the line is a buried electrical conduit for a tank heater: do not pour water on an electrical freeze — check the breaker first.
STOP if animals are without water and you cannot thaw the line in an hour: haul water from another source first, thaw second.

title: Make a float valve for a stock tank from a plastic bottle
mechanism_check: A float valve is a lever: rising water lifts the float, and the lever arm multiplies that small force to close the inlet against line pressure.
The seal closes only if the lever geometry puts the float's travel in line with the valve seat — wrong angles jam instead of closing.
Debris in the seat is the failure mode: unfiltered supply water holds the valve open a hair and the tank overflows all night.
improvised_tools: A 1- or 2-liter plastic bottle as the float
A stiff wire or flat metal strip as the lever arm
A rubber washer or inner-tube scrap as the valve seat seal
Hose clamps, screws, and a drilled cap for the inlet
steps: Drill the inlet through the tank wall or a feed pipe at the target water level; fit the seat so the seal washer presses square against the inlet.
Mount the lever arm on a pivot screw above the seat: the bottle hangs on the long end, the seal washer on the short end.
Adjust the arm so the bottle lifts the washer fully onto the seat when the water reaches your level mark.
Weight or half-fill the bottle if it rides too high and closes the valve early.
Filter the supply line with a screen: grit in the seat defeats the whole valve.
Test by draining the tank halfway and watching a full fill cycle — the valve must shut off dead, not dribble.
stop_conditions: STOP if the supply is a high-pressure municipal line: a homemade float cannot safely hold more than a few psi — buy a real valve.
STOP if the valve will not fully close during the test: do not leave it unattended or the tank overflows.
STOP if the float arm binds on the tank wall: rework the geometry until travel is free through the whole range.
STOP if the tank serves as the only water source: keep a backup supply until the float proves itself for a full week.

title: Repair a flat wheelbarrow tire with an inner-tube patch or solid fill
mechanism_check: A wheelbarrow flat is almost never a blown tire — it is a slow bead leak or a thorn puncture in the tube, and the fix depends on which one you find.
Patches bond to the tube, not the tire: the tube must be clean and dry or the patch lifts on the first load.
Solid foam fill eliminates flats permanently but adds weight and changes the ride — a tradeoff worth naming before you commit.
improvised_tools: A patch kit, or a tire plug kit for tubeless tires
Soapy water in a bucket to find the leak
Tire levers, screwdrivers, or flat bars to break the bead
A pump or compressor; rags to dry the tube
steps: Remove the wheel and submerge the inflated tube (or tire) in soapy water; mark every bubble source.
If tubeless and the leak is a thorn hole, ream it and plug it with the kit — fastest fix available.
If tubed, pull the tube, roughen and clean the puncture area, and apply the patch per the kit's cure time — rush the cure and the patch fails.
Reseat the bead, inflate to the sidewall pressure, and re-check in soapy water.
Consider foam-fill sealant as a permanent upgrade if flats are chronic on thorny ground.
Reinstall the wheel and check the axle bolt — flats hide loose hardware.
stop_conditions: STOP if the tire sidewall is cracked through or the rim is bent: patching a failed casing is false economy — replace the wheel.
STOP if the tube has more than three patches or a split: tubes are cheap, reliability is not.
STOP if the bead will not seat after two tries: deflate fully and reseat from scratch rather than over-inflating — a bead popping at 60 psi is dangerous.
STOP if foam fill is going on a wheelbarrow used on slopes: the added weight changes handling on hills.

title: Build a hay feeder that cuts waste from scrap lumber
mechanism_check: Hay waste comes from animals pulling hay out and dropping it on the ground, then refusing it: waste is a geometry problem, not an animal problem.
The fix is a head-space that lets an animal reach in but not climb in, and a tray that catches what drops so it stays feedable.
Wet hay rots from the bottom: any feeder design must drain or elevate the hay off the ground.
improvised_tools: Scrap 2x4s, pallets, or deck boards for the frame
A cattle panel or hog panel section for the feeding face
Screws or nails; a saw
A plywood or metal sheet offcut for the roof
steps: Size the feeder to the animal: cattle need a 24-inch reach depth, sheep and goats need vertical slats they cannot climb through.
Build a raised box with slatted sides animals eat through, and a solid catch tray 6 inches below the slat bottom.
Keep the eating height at chest level: too low and they stand in it, too high and small stock cannot reach.
Roof it: rain on open hay turns the top layer to compost and doubles waste.
Site it on a pad of gravel or packed earth that drains — mud under a feeder is a hoof-rot factory.
Anchor or weight it: cattle will push an unanchored feeder across the paddock.
stop_conditions: STOP if the slat spacing can trap a head: test with the smallest animal — head-entrapment kills stock.
STOP if the design lets animals climb inside: a manger they stand in becomes a contamination and injury site.
STOP if you are feeding horned animals through fixed slats: use adjustable or removable bars so horns do not lock in a panic.
STOP if the feeder will sit in a flood zone: relocate before the first storm, not after.

title: Tie stock-proof knots for gate ropes and lead ties
mechanism_check: A knot holds by friction under load: wraps around the standing line create the friction, and the tail locks them in.
The failure mode of a stock knot is not slipping under load — it is jamming when you need it UNDONE fast with a panicking animal.
Quick-release knots (the slip or bowline family) trade a little strength for the ability to free an animal with one pull.
improvised_tools: Rope, lead line, or baling twine for practice
A post or fence rail to tie around
A knife to cut and re-try without untying knots
Gloves while learning — rope burn teaches faster than any warning
steps: Learn the bowline first: the loop that will not slip closed around a neck or leg — practice until you can tie it blindfold.
Learn the quick-release (slip) hitch for tying to posts: one pull frees the animal.
Tie leads to the post at head height, never low: a low tie lets an animal get a leg over the rope.
Leave enough tail that the knot cannot work loose, and check knots daily — rope shrinks and loosens with weather.
Replace any rope that is sun-rotted or frayed: a knot in bad rope is decoration.
Practice untying under tension with gloves on: the test of a stock knot is the release, not the tie.
stop_conditions: STOP tying with any knot you cannot untie one-handed while wearing gloves — that is the standard.
STOP if the animal is already panicking: approach, calm, then tie — never wrestle a knot into a thrashing animal.
STOP using twine or thin cord on large stock: it cuts into necks and legs when it tightens.
STOP if the tie point is a weak board or loose wire: a tied animal that breaks free takes the fence with it.

title: Improvise a poultry waterer from a 5-gallon bucket and nipples
mechanism_check: Nipple drinkers work on vacuum and gravity: the bucket seals, and each peck opens a valve that releases a drop — no standing water, no drowning, no algae.
The failure mode is air leaks: any hole above the water line or a cracked lid breaks the vacuum and the bucket drains through the lowest nipple.
Nipples must be at beak height for the bird: too high and chicks cannot reach, too low and bedding fouls the mechanism.
improvised_tools: A 5-gallon food-grade bucket with a tight lid
Screw-in poultry nipples (or order them — they are cheap and worth it)
A drill with the nipple-size bit
A hanging chain or wire, and a catch tray
steps: Drill nipple holes in the bottom or lower side wall of the bucket, spaced 6 inches apart.
Thread the nipples in with their rubber seals; hand-tight plus a quarter turn — overtightening cracks the plastic.
Fill the bucket, snap the lid on TIGHT, and hang it so nipples sit at the birds' beak height.
Tap each nipple to prime it and confirm a drop forms and stops.
Place a shallow catch tray under the bucket to keep bedding dry from the inevitable dribble.
Scrub and refill weekly; check nipples for sticking open after freezing weather.
stop_conditions: STOP if the bucket will not seal airtight: the vacuum system will not work — find a bucket with a real gasket lid.
STOP if chicks are under a week old: day-olds need an open dish they can find by instinct before transitioning to nipples.
STOP if nipples leak continuously: the seat is damaged or installed crooked — replace the nipple, not the bucket.
STOP if the waterer is the only source in a heat wave: keep a backup open pan until the birds reliably use the nipples.

title: Dig and line a swale to redirect runoff away from the barn
mechanism_check: A swale is a wide, shallow ditch that slows water and moves it sideways across a slope — depth makes gullies, width makes swales.
Water follows the path of least resistance: the swale only works if its outlet is LOWER than its inlet, measured with a level, not by eye.
Unlined swales on bare soil erode into gullies in one hard storm: grass, stone, or fabric armoring is the actual structure.
improvised_tools: Shovels, a mattock, or a rented trencher for long runs
A line level and stakes to check the fall
Grass seed, straw, or riprap stone for armoring
Landscape fabric or salvaged geotextile for the channel bed
steps: Watch one real rainstorm and mark where the water actually goes — design from observation, not assumption.
Stake the swale line across the slope with a steady fall (1-2 percent) away from the barn toward a safe outlet.
Dig a broad, shallow channel — 2 feet wide, 6 inches deep beats 1 foot wide and 1 foot deep.
Line the channel with fabric or stone where the flow concentrates, and seed or sod the rest immediately.
Build a small berm on the downhill lip to keep overflow from short-circuiting the channel.
Walk it after the next storm and fix any scour spots before they grow.
stop_conditions: STOP if the outlet would flood a neighbor's land or a septic field: reroute or get agreement first.
STOP if you are diverting a real stream or wetland drainage: check local regulations before touching it.
STOP if the swale crosses a buried utility path: call for a locate before digging.
STOP if the barn foundation is already undermined: a swale is prevention, not repair — stabilize the foundation first.

title: Restore a rusted hand tool with a vinegar soak and re-sharpening
mechanism_check: Rust is iron oxide on the surface: vinegar (acetic acid) dissolves it without removing base metal, unlike grinding which thins the tool.
The cutting geometry is what makes a tool work: removing rust changes nothing if the bevel angle is wrong or the edge is rolled.
Flash rust forms within hours of a vinegar soak: the tool must be neutralized, dried, and oiled immediately after derusting.
improvised_tools: White vinegar in a bucket or tray for the soak
A wire brush, steel wool, or sandpaper for scrubbing
Baking soda and water for neutralizing the acid
Boiled linseed oil or motor oil for the finish
steps: Knock off loose rust and dirt with the wire brush first — the soak handles what is bonded.
Submerge the head in vinegar for 4-12 hours; check progress, not the clock.
Scrub off the loosened black rust with steel wool; repeat the soak if deep pitting remains.
Rinse in baking-soda water to neutralize the acid, then dry completely — heat helps.
Restore the factory bevel with a file: edge tools get their angle back before they get their sharpness.
Oil the whole head and the handle end; hang the tool up, never store it on damp concrete.
stop_conditions: STOP if pitting is deeper than the edge bevel can clean up: a pitted edge will never hold sharpness — the tool is done.
STOP if the tool head is cracked: derusting a cracked head makes a prettier hazard.
STOP if the vinegar soak runs over 24 hours: acid starts eating base metal and weakening thin edges.
STOP if you plan to store it in the same damp spot: fix the storage or the rust returns in a season.

title: Build a predator-deterrent night pen for lambs and kids from panels
mechanism_check: Night losses happen because small stock sleep in the open where coyotes and dogs cruise: the pen's job is making the sleeping area impenetrable for 8 dark hours.
A pen works by removal of opportunity: panels stop the rush, a roof or cover stops the climb, and a guardian or light changes the risk calculus.
The failure point is always a gap at ground level or a panel an animal can push: predators test the perimeter, not the middle.
improvised_tools: Cattle or hog panels, or a stock trailer as one wall
T-posts to anchor the panels
A tarp, netting, or wire top as an overhead cover
A motion light or radio as a deterrent
steps: Site the pen on high ground near the house or barn — proximity to humans is itself a deterrent.
Stand panels in a tight rectangle, 16x16 feet minimum for a small group, anchored with t-posts every 8 feet.
Wire or clamp panel joints so they cannot be pushed apart; anchor the bottom edge to the ground with stakes.
Cover the top with tarp or netting: coyotes climb panels, dogs jump them.
Herd the lambs/kids in at dusk with feed as the lure; lock the gate and check the latch.
Put a motion light or a talk-radio station at the pen — sound and light are cheap force multipliers.
stop_conditions: STOP if the pen is smaller than the group needs: overcrowding causes trampling and pneumonia — size for the whole group or split them.
STOP if there is no overhead cover and coyotes are the local threat: panels alone are a suggestion to a coyote.
STOP if the gate cannot be latched against a dog's push: a pen is only as good as its gate.
STOP if bedding gets wet and stays wet: move or re-bed the pen, or you trade predation for disease.

title: Build a portable chicken tractor from conduit and wire
mechanism_check: A chicken tractor is a floorless pen that moves daily: the birds get fresh forage and the ground gets fertilized, but only if the tractor is light enough to actually move.
Lightness and rigidity fight each other: conduit frames are stiff per pound, which is why they beat lumber for portable designs.
The drag edge must sit flush on the ground: any gap is an exit for chicks and an entry for rats.
improvised_tools: Electrical conduit or PVC for the frame (conduit is stronger per pound)
Chicken wire or welded wire for the sides and top
Zip ties, hose clamps, or wire for frame joints
A tarp for the sheltered third and a handle or rope for pulling
steps: Bend or joint conduit into two A-frame or hoop ends; connect them with straight runs to make a 4x8 or 6x10 foot box.
Wire the sides and one end; leave one end as a liftable door for access and moving birds.
Cover the back third with the tarp as the weather shelter and shade — the open two-thirds is the forage zone.
Add a pull handle at the front and a drag skirt of wire at the bottom edge, bent outward to sit flat.
Move the tractor one length each morning BEFORE feeding: the birds follow the feed and forage the fresh strip.
Rest each patch 3-4 weeks before the tractor returns: that is the parasite break the system depends on.
stop_conditions: STOP if the frame is too heavy to move by one person: you will stop moving it, and then it is just a pen.
STOP if the wire has gaps bigger than 1 inch at chick level: chicks will exit and rats will enter.
STOP if hawks are the local threat and there is no top cover: add the tarp over the whole tractor or lose birds.
STOP if the ground is waterlogged: move the tractor to high ground — wet bedding under a tractor is a disease trap.

title: Mix a homemade fly spray for livestock from essential oils
mechanism_check: Fly repellents work by masking the CO2 and odor cues flies home in on — the spray changes the animal's scent signature, not the flies' biology.
Oil-based carriers stick to hair and last hours; water-based sprays run off in minutes — the carrier is the delivery system.
Essential oils are concentrated plant chemistry: the dose that repels flies is close to the dose that irritates skin, so dilution is the safety margin.
improvised_tools: Cedarwood, citronella, lemongrass, or eucalyptus essential oil
A carrier: apple cider vinegar, witch hazel, or vegetable oil
A spray bottle
Gloves for mixing
steps: Mix 2 tablespoons of carrier oil or 1 cup of vinegar/witch hazel with 15-20 drops TOTAL of essential oil per pint of spray.
Shake hard before every use — oil and water separate, and an unshaken bottle sprays a hot slug of pure oil.
Patch-test on one animal's neck: spray a small area, wait 24 hours, check for redness or rubbing.
Apply to the body, legs, and belly; avoid eyes, nose, udders, and any open wound.
Reapply every few hours in heavy fly pressure; it wears off faster than commercial permethrin.
Label the bottle with the recipe and date; make fresh every two weeks.
stop_conditions: STOP if any animal shows redness, swelling, rubbing, or distress after the patch test: do not use that oil on your stock.
STOP using tea tree (melaleuca) oil on cats, and keep it away from poultry — it is toxic to them.
STOP spraying near eyes, muzzles, udders, and wounds: irritants there cause real harm.
STOP relying on homemade spray during a disease-vector fly outbreak (pinkeye, etc.): this is repellent, not treatment — call a vet.

title: Build a raised garden bed from reclaimed lumber
mechanism_check: A raised bed works by giving roots deep, loose, warm soil: the frame is just a container, the soil mix is the product.
Depth beats width: 10-12 inches of good soil grows more than 6 inches of anything — shallow beds dry out and stunt roots.
Untreated or naturally rot-resistant wood is the constraint: treated lumber chemistry leaches into food soil.
improvised_tools: Reclaimed boards, pallets (HT stamp), or logs for the frame
Screws or nails; a saw
Cardboard or newspaper for the weed barrier
Compost, topsoil, and mulch for the fill
steps: Pick a sunny, level spot with water access; 4 feet wide is the max you can reach across from both sides.
Lay cardboard directly on the grass as a weed barrier — it smothers the sod and rots into the soil.
Stack boards to 10-12 inches high, screwing corners together; stake the sides if they bow.
Fill with a mix of topsoil and compost, mounding slightly — it will settle 2 inches in a month.
Mulch the surface 3 inches deep to hold moisture and suppress weeds.
Plant, and plan to top-dress with compost every season: the bed eats its own soil.
stop_conditions: STOP if the lumber is painted with old lead paint or is railroad-tie creosote: do not grow food in contact with it.
STOP if pallets are marked MB (methyl bromide): same rule as the compost bins.
STOP if the site has no drainage and holds standing water: the bed becomes a bathtub — fix drainage first.
STOP if you cannot water it regularly: a raised bed dries faster than ground soil and punishes neglect.

title: Improvise a fence-post brace (H-brace) without concrete
mechanism_check: A corner or end post takes the full pull of the fence line: a single post cannot resist it — the H-brace turns two posts and a horizontal rail into a truss that cannot lean.
The diagonal tension wire is the actual structure: it converts the leaning force into compression on the rail, which wood handles beautifully.
Concrete is optional: a driven H-brace with a proper diagonal wire outlasts a concreted single post, because concrete locks a post that still wants to move.
improvised_tools: Two posts (wood or t-post) and a horizontal rail for the H
Brace wire, smooth wire, or cable for the diagonal
A stick or ratchet to twist the diagonal tight
A shovel for setting the second post
steps: Set the end post and a second post 8 feet in-line, both driven to full depth and plumb (see homestead-011).
Fit the horizontal rail between them at two-thirds height, notched or wired so it cannot slip down.
Run the diagonal wire from the top of the end post to the bottom of the second post — this is the critical direction: it must oppose the fence pull.
Twist the diagonal tight with a stick windlass until it sings; the rail should be in solid compression.
Hang the fence line off the END post only; the second post exists to serve the brace.
Check the diagonal twice a year: wire stretches, and a loose diagonal is a leaning corner.
stop_conditions: STOP if the diagonal wire runs the wrong way (top of second post to bottom of end post): it will actively pull the corner over — reverse it.
STOP if either post is in a wet hole or mud: set in firm ground or the truss pivots as a unit.
STOP if you are bracing for high-tensile wire: double the H (two braces) for runs over 300 feet.
STOP if the rail is green and flexing: use a seasoned rail or double up — the truss is only as stiff as its compression member.

title: Repair a sagging gate by re-hanging it with a tension cable
mechanism_check: A gate sags because its own weight twists the frame into a parallelogram: the top far corner drops while the hinge side stays put.
A diagonal cable from the top hinge corner to the bottom latch corner converts the sag back into a rectangle — the cable carries tension, the frame carries compression.
Tightening a cable on a frame with failed joints just pulls the joints apart: the frame must be sound before the cable goes on.
improvised_tools: Steel cable, wire rope, or braided fence wire for the diagonal
Turnbuckle, or a wire twister/stick for tensioning
Eye bolts or lag screws for the cable anchors
Wrenches or pliers
steps: Lift the gate to true level and block it there with sawhorses or blocks — tension the cable with the gate already straight.
Check every frame joint: re-screw, re-nail, or re-bolt any loose joint before adding the cable.
Run the cable from the top hinge-side corner to the bottom latch-side corner, anchored with eye bolts.
Tension with the turnbuckle (or twist the wire tight) until the gate holds level on its own when the blocks are kicked away.
Re-hang the hinges if the post has leaned (see homestead-003 for hinge rebuilds).
Re-check tension seasonally: wood shrinks and cables stretch.
stop_conditions: STOP if the frame joints are rotted: a cable cannot save a rotten frame — rebuild or replace the gate.
STOP if the hinge post itself is leaning: fix the post first (see homestead-026) or the sag returns in a week.
STOP if the cable is undersized twine or thin wire: it will stretch and snap under a stock gate's weight — use real cable.
STOP if the gate drags the ground after tensioning: the frame is twisted, not just sagged — rebuild the frame square.

title: Build a treadle feeder from a bucket to defeat rats
mechanism_check: A treadle feeder works on weight discrimination: a chicken (4+ pounds) steps the treadle open, a rat (under a pound) cannot.
The mechanism is a lever with a counterweight or spring: the treadle must move freely through its full arc or the lid binds half-open — which is worse than no lid.
Rats defeat feeders by reach, not weight: the feed tray must sit far enough back that a rat on the treadle edge cannot stretch to it.
improvised_tools: A 5-gallon bucket or metal trash can with a lid
A plywood or sheet-metal treadle plate
Hinge, rod, or wire for the treadle pivot
A counterweight (rocks, scrap metal) or bungee for the return spring
steps: Cut a feed-access slot in the bucket side, set back 4 inches from the front — the setback is the rat-proofing.
Mount the treadle plate on a pivot in front of the slot, linked to the lid or a sliding door over the slot.
Set the counterweight so the treadle needs 2-3 pounds to open: test with a bag of feed before any bird tries it.
Train the flock: prop the lid half-open for two days, then quarter-open, letting hunger teach them to step on.
Check the pivot weekly for bedding and manure binding the mechanism.
Keep the feeder under cover: rain plus feed equals a cemented mechanism.
stop_conditions: STOP if the treadle opens with less than a pound of pressure: rats will feast — add counterweight.
STOP if the lid snaps shut on a bird's head during training: pad or slow the return until the flock is trained.
STOP if bantams or small chicks cannot open it: this design is for standard-size birds — bantams need a lighter setting.
STOP if rats are chewing through the bucket: switch to a metal can body — plastic is a delay, not a barrier.

title: Build a vermicompost worm bin from stacked totes
mechanism_check: Red wigglers eat bedding and scraps from the top down and migrate UP toward fresh food: stacked totes exploit this — finished castings sit in the bottom tote, worms in the top.
The system fails on moisture balance: too wet and it goes anaerobic (smell), too dry and the worms die — wrung-sponge dampness is the target.
Worms breathe through their skin: no air holes means dead worms, and dead worms mean a rotten bin.
improvised_tools: Two or three stackable totes with lids
A drill for air and drainage holes
Shredded cardboard, newspaper, or coconut coir for bedding
A pound of red wigglers to start
steps: Drill 1/4-inch air holes around the top tote's upper walls and 1/8-inch drainage holes in the bottom totes.
Fill the top tote two-thirds with damp shredded cardboard bedding, fluffed, not packed.
Add the worms and a handful of kitchen scraps buried under the bedding — start feeding light.
Stack: top tote is the active bin, lower totes catch drainage (leachate — dilute it 10:1 for plants).
Feed weekly, burying scraps under bedding; no meat, dairy, or oily food.
When the top tote is mostly castings, set a fresh bedding tote on top — worms migrate up, and you harvest the bottom.
stop_conditions: STOP if the bin smells rotten: it is too wet or overfed — stop feeding, add dry bedding, and drain it.
STOP if worms are massing at the lid trying to escape: something is wrong (too wet, too acidic, too hot) — fix conditions before adding food.
STOP placing the bin in direct sun or where it freezes: worms die above 85F and below 40F.
STOP if fruit flies swarm: bury food deeper and cover the surface with dry bedding.

title: Patch a torn pond or tank liner with EPDM tape
mechanism_check: EPDM liner patches bond chemically: the primer softens the liner surface and the tape fuses to it — this is a weld, not a sticker.
The bond fails on contamination: algae film, silt, and sunscreen residue all prevent fusion, and the failure shows up months later as a slow weep.
Water pressure pushes the patch ONTO the liner from inside, so patches go on the water side — outside patches peel.
improvised_tools: EPDM seam tape and primer (the real materials — no substitute bonds reliably)
Scouring pad and clean rags
A roller, rolling pin, or smooth bottle for pressing the patch
A marker to outline the patch area
steps: Drain or lower the water below the tear; the patch area must be dry for the primer.
Scrub the liner 3 inches past the tear in all directions; rinse and let dry completely.
Apply primer to liner and patch, let it flash to tacky (follow the product's timing — this is the step people rush).
Lay the patch on the WATER side, roll it down hard from the center out to push out every air bubble.
Weight or clamp the patch for the cure time on the product label.
Refill slowly and watch the patch under pressure for a day before trusting it.
stop_conditions: STOP if the liner is sun-rotted and tearing in multiple places: patching lace is futile — replace the liner.
STOP if you cannot get the area dry: primer will not flash on a wet surface — pump it down or wait.
STOP using duct tape, silicone, or roofing tar as liner patches: none bond to EPDM and all fail underwater.
STOP if the tear is at a folded stress point: add a larger patch that bridges past the fold, or the tear reopens at the edge.

title: Run the homestead on a seasonal planning calendar
mechanism_check: A homestead fails by missed timing, not by lack of effort: planting windows, breeding cycles, and maintenance tasks all have hard deadlines set by weather and biology.
The planning failure mode is carrying the whole calendar in one head — when that person is sick or busy, the system collapses.
A wall calendar works because it externalizes memory: anyone in the household can see what is due without asking.
improvised_tools: A large wall calendar or a whiteboard divided into 12 months
A different color marker per domain: garden, livestock, buildings, money
A notebook for the observations that do not fit on the calendar
A yearly review ritual (one evening in winter) to update the calendar from what you learned
steps: Divide the calendar into quarters and block the immovable dates first: average last frost, first frost, breeding windows, tax dates.
Add recurring maintenance by season: fence walking in spring, water-system winterizing in fall, tool servicing in winter.
Assign each block an owner by name — 'the garden' is nobody's job; 'Maria — garden beds' is a job.
Put the calendar where work starts (barn door, kitchen) — a plan nobody sees is decoration.
Review weekly in season: 10 minutes to move what slipped and reassign what stalled.
In winter, run the review ritual: cross out what did not pay, double down on what did, and date the next year's blocks.
stop_conditions: STOP if the calendar has no named owners: anonymous tasks do not get done — assign or delete.
STOP if more than three tasks slip two weeks in a row: the plan is overloaded — cut scope, not sleep.
STOP adding detail nobody will read: if the calendar needs a legend to decode, simplify it.
STOP if one person owns everything: rebalance before resentment does it for you.

title: Keep a soil observation journal through the growing season
mechanism_check: Soil improvement is a multi-year feedback loop: you only learn what worked if you record what you did and what you saw.
Memory lies about gardens: every grower remembers the harvest and forgets the week of yellow leaves in June that predicted it.
The journal works by pairing an action (amendment, till, mulch) with a dated observation — without both halves, it is a diary, not data.
improvised_tools: A weatherproof notebook or a phone with a notes app
A mason jar for the free soil-texture test (shake soil in water, watch layers settle)
A pH test kit or strips
A camera for dated bed photos — one photo per bed per month
steps: At season start, write one line per bed: what is planted, what amendment went in, the date.
Walk the garden weekly with the notebook: note color, vigor, pests, moisture — two minutes per bed.
Run the jar test once per new bed and log the sand/silt/clay layers; retest only after major amendments.
Log every input (compost, lime, manure) with amount and date — this is the half everyone skips.
Photograph each bed monthly from the same spot; compare photos at season end, not memory.
In winter, read the journal against the harvest: decide next year's amendments from the record, not from habit.
stop_conditions: STOP if entries are vague ('looks okay'): an unmeasurable observation is not data — record color, height, dates.
STOP buying amendments until the journal shows a pattern: guessing chemistry is how soil gets worse.
STOP if the journal lives in a drawer: move it to the potting bench or it will not survive May.
STOP if pH is untested after three years of amendments: test before adding more lime or sulfur — you may be fixing a problem you caused.

title: Run a daily livestock check routine that catches trouble early
mechanism_check: Livestock are prey animals: they hide illness until they cannot, so by the time a problem is obvious it is advanced — the check routine exists to catch the pre-obvious stage.
The routine works by comparison: you are not diagnosing, you are noticing who is different from yesterday — appetite, movement, manure, water intake.
Skipped days are the failure mode: problems found Monday that started Saturday are emergencies, not treatments.
improvised_tools: A fixed route: same order, same time, every day
A pocket notebook or a whiteboard at the barn for logging anomalies
A thermometer and a stethoscope in the barn kit
A phone for photographing anything odd — lameness, swelling, discharge
steps: Walk the route in the same order: feed, water, then eyes on every animal — count heads against the known number.
Watch for the four tells: not eating, separated from the group, limping, abnormal manure.
Log anything off with a date; one line is enough — the log is what turns a hunch into a timeline.
Check water flow and feed levels as part of the route, not as a separate chore.
Isolate any animal that is off feed or visibly ill before you finish the route — minutes matter more than certainty.
Call the vet when the timeline shows two days of decline or any single alarming sign (bloat, down animal, labor trouble).
stop_conditions: STOP the routine from becoming a glance: if you finished in five minutes, you skipped the looking — redo it.
STOP treating from memory: check the log for what you already tried before dosing again.
STOP if you are unsure and the animal is declining: a vet call beats a guess every time.
STOP skipping days during weather stress, lambing, or kidding season: that is when the routine matters most.

title: Make the homestead pay: turn surplus into a cashflow ledger
mechanism_check: Homesteads bleed money on inputs and give away outputs: the ledger makes the real margin visible, and the margin decides what survives.
The failure mode is romance accounting — counting the eggs sold and ignoring the feed bill, the fencing, and the hours.
Pricing works by knowing your true cost per unit first: market price means nothing until you know what the dozen eggs actually cost you to produce.
improvised_tools: A simple ledger: notebook, spreadsheet, or an app — one page per enterprise (eggs, meat birds, garden, firewood)
A kitchen scale for weighing harvests
A running list of input costs: feed, seed, fuel, replacement stock
A market survey: what do local buyers actually pay, recorded with dates
steps: List every homestead enterprise separately: eggs, broilers, garden surplus, firewood, honey, whatever you sell or could sell.
Track one full cycle of inputs per enterprise: every bag of feed, every seed packet, fuel, and your hours at a wage you choose.
Weigh and count every output for the same cycle: dozens, pounds, cords.
Compute true cost per unit; price above it or stop doing that enterprise — sentiment is not a business plan.
Sell where the margin is: farm gate, market, or neighbors — test all three for one month and keep the winner.
Review quarterly against the seasonal calendar (homestead-041): cut the lowest-margin enterprise, feed the winner.
stop_conditions: STOP any enterprise whose true cost exceeds its price for two cycles: it is a hobby, not income — label it honestly.
STOP scaling what you have not tracked: doubling an unmeasured enterprise doubles the loss.
STOP if you cannot name your buyer before you produce: growing first and selling later is how barns fill with unsold squash.
STOP before taking on debt for an enterprise: prove the margin at small scale first.

title: Run a tool maintenance rotation so nothing fails in season
mechanism_check: Tools fail at the worst moment because maintenance is deferred to 'later' and later never comes during planting or harvest.
A rotation works by moving maintenance to the off-season per tool class: each tool gets serviced when it is idle, not when it is needed.
The failure mode is the unknown-broken tool: the chainsaw that has not run since October and will not start on the day the tree falls on the fence.
improvised_tools: A maintenance chart: one row per tool, columns for clean, sharpen, oil, test-run
Winter evenings as the service window
Consumables on hand: bar oil, files, spark plugs, shear pins
A 'dead' shelf: anything broken goes there immediately, tagged with what is wrong
steps: Inventory every powered and cutting tool; write each on the chart with its service needs.
Schedule service by idle season: mowers and tillers in winter, chainsaws in summer, fencing tools after fence season.
Service each tool fully: clean, sharpen (see homestead-010, homestead-021), oil, replace wear parts, test-run.
Anything broken goes to the dead shelf with a tag — never back on the working shelf to ambush you later.
Stock the consumables that strand you: shear pins, spark plugs, files, bar oil — the five-dollar part that costs a day.
Re-test every tool two weeks before its season starts: the shakedown catches what the bench missed.
stop_conditions: STOP running a tool that failed its test-run: fix it now or rent/borrow — a dying tool dies mid-job.
STOP if the dead shelf grows past three items: schedule a repair day before the pile becomes permanent.
STOP using a tool with a disabled safety (chain brake, blade guard): the guard is part of the tool.
STOP if you have no manual for a tool: find it online before disassembly, not during.

title: Save seed and select varieties for your own ground
mechanism_check: Seed saving is selection: every generation you keep seed from, the plants adapt a little more to your soil, your pests, your season length.
Open-pollinated varieties breed true; hybrids (F1) do not — saving hybrid seed gives you unpredictable offspring, which is the classic beginner heartbreak.
Isolation is the mechanism: squash and corn cross-pollinate across varieties, so saved seed needs distance or hand-pollination to stay true.
improvised_tools: Open-pollinated seed stock to start from
Paper bags and labeled envelopes for drying and storing seed
A journal entry per variety (links to the soil journal, homestead-042)
A cool, dry, dark storage spot — a sealed jar in a closet works
steps: Start with open-pollinated varieties of self-pollinating crops (tomatoes, beans, lettuce) — easiest wins first.
Mark your best plants mid-season with ribbon: earliest, healthiest, best-flavored — save seed from THOSE, not from the average.
Let seed mature fully on the plant; wet-process tomato seed (ferment 3 days, rinse, dry), dry-process beans and lettuce on the plant.
Dry seed to cracker-crisp, label with variety and year, store cool and dark.
Grow out your saved seed next year and compare against the journal: select again from the best — that is the adaptation loop.
Add cross-pollinators (squash, corn) only when you can manage isolation: 800 feet, or bag-and-hand-pollinate.
stop_conditions: STOP saving seed from diseased plants: you are selecting FOR the disease.
STOP if varieties crossed and you cannot verify purity: eat the harvest, do not sell the seed as the variety.
STOP storing damp seed: mold kills germination — if it bends instead of snapping, dry it more.
STOP after three generations of saving from weak stock: buy fresh open-pollinated seed and restart selection.

title: Run a whole-homestead winterizing sweep as one system
mechanism_check: Winter damage is a systems failure: the pipe that bursts, the roof that leaks under snow load, and the animal without windbreak all fail from the same missed walkthrough.
A sweep works because it is one pass through every system with a checklist — piecemeal winterizing misses the thing you forgot existed.
The sweep must happen before the first hard freeze, not during: frozen ground and frozen hands turn a two-hour job into a crisis.
improvised_tools: A winterizing checklist, one section per system: water, shelter, feed, fuel, power, access
Insulation materials: foam, feed sacks, straw bales
A fuel and feed inventory count
A snow-day access plan: which gates, which paths, where the plow or shovel goes first
steps: Walk the water system end to end: drain hoses, insulate risers, test tank heaters, verify the well house stays above freezing.
Walk every animal shelter: windbreaks up, bedding deep, roof sound, gates swinging free (frozen gates trap animals).
Count feed and fuel against the winter: order the shortfall now, when delivery is easy.
Service the generator: test-run under load, fuel stabilized, extension cords located.
Clear and mark access paths: which gate gets shoveled first, where the truck turns, where the snow piles go.
Do the sweep on the calendar (homestead-041) as a fixed annual date — the same weekend every year.
stop_conditions: STOP if the first freeze is forecast within 48 hours and the sweep is not done: triage to water and shelter only, defer the rest.
STOP winterizing with the animals locked out of their shelter: finish one shelter fully before starting the next.
STOP if the roof shows structural sag under last year's snow memory: a sweep does not fix a failing roof — repair it now.
STOP if feed inventory is under 60 days: order immediately; winter delivery failures are how herds go hungry.

title: Hold a ten-minute morning crew huddle before work starts
mechanism_check: Farm crews fail by assumption: two people doing the same job while a third job goes undone, because nobody said the plan out loud.
The huddle works by making the day's plan common knowledge in one short loop — priorities, assignments, hazards — before anyone picks up a tool.
It fails when it becomes a lecture: the moment one person talks and everyone else zones out, the huddle is theater.
improvised_tools: A fixed time and place: same spot, same time, every workday
A whiteboard or a scrap of plywood with today's three priorities
A round-robin format: each person states their task, their blocker, and any hazard they see
A one-minute weather and animal-status check to open
steps: Gather at the fixed spot — barn door, tailgate, kitchen table — before tools come out.
State the day's three priorities in order: what must happen, what should happen, what can wait.
Go around the circle: each person names their task, what they need, and any hazard (loose bull, broken gate, storm coming).
Reassign on the spot when someone is blocked or a priority shifted overnight.
End with the safety minute: today's specific risk, named out loud.
Keep it to ten minutes: if it runs long, the plan was not ready — prepare it the night before.
stop_conditions: STOP if the same person talks and nobody else speaks for a week: the huddle is broken — ask directly what is wrong.
STOP if assignments are ignored after the huddle: the problem is authority, not communication — settle who decides.
STOP adding agenda items: anything needing more than two minutes becomes a separate conversation after the huddle.
STOP holding the huddle if there is no work plan: a huddle without a plan is a meeting about nothing — skip it and plan first.

title: Triage storm damage as a crew without making it worse
mechanism_check: After a storm, the urge is to fix everything at once: the crew scatters, nobody secures anything, and the second wave of damage (loose stock, live wires, unstable trees) does the real harm.
Triage works by sequencing: secure living things, secure hazards, then secure property — in that order, every time.
The coordination failure is freelancing: one person cutting a tree across the fence line another person is repairing.
improvised_tools: A triage leader for the day — one voice giving the order, rotating by who is calmest, not by rank
A walkthrough route: animals first, then hazards, then buildings, then fences
Roles assigned on the spot: animal handler, hazard spotter, tool runner
A phone or radio check-in every 30 minutes if the crew splits up
steps: Leader does a silent walkthrough first — no tools, no fixing — and lists damage in triage order: animals, hazards (wires, leaning trees, gas), buildings, fences.
Contain loose or injured animals before anything else: a loose bull in a storm zone outranks a broken barn door.
Mark hazards with flagging or rope: do not work under a hung-up limb or near a downed line — mark it and move on.
Assign pairs, never solo, for hazard work: the spotter's only job is watching the cutter's surroundings.
Repair in triage order, and keep one person as runner so workers are not leaving their posts to fetch tools.
Debrief at the end of the day: what broke, what held, what to harden before the next storm.
stop_conditions: STOP all work if lightning is still active or winds are still dangerous: no fence is worth a strike.
STOP cutting any tree touching a power line or structure: call the utility or a pro — storm-loaded trees kill experienced cutters.
STOP if anyone is injured: the triage list freezes until the person is cared for.
STOP freelancing: if the plan changed, return to the leader before starting a new task — uncoordinated help is a hazard.

title: Coordinate a harvest-day crew so nothing waits on anything
mechanism_check: Harvest is a pipeline: picking, hauling, processing, storing — the day fails at the bottleneck stage, and the bottleneck is wherever the fewest hands are.
The crew fails by everyone doing the fun part (picking) while the unglamorous stage (hauling, washing) starves — work piles up at the bottleneck and rots.
Throughput is set by the slowest stage: adding pickers when hauling is the bottleneck makes the pile bigger, not the day shorter.
improvised_tools: A harvest-day role chart: picker, hauler, processor, storer — one lead per stage
The morning huddle (homestead-048) to assign stages by strength and skill
Staging areas: full crates go HERE, empties go THERE — marked with chalk or tape
A mid-day check: 15 minutes to rebalance the crew to the bottleneck
steps: The night before, stage every container, tool, and wash station: harvest day starts with zero setup.
In the huddle, assign each person a stage, not a crop — stages are the pipeline.
Start all stages at once: the first pickers' crates must meet a hauler, not a pile.
Run the mid-day rebalance: find where product is piling up, move hands there until it clears.
Rotate the heavy stages after lunch: hauling and processing trade crews so nobody breaks.
End-of-day: everything picked is processed or stored before anyone leaves — picked-and-piled is picked-and-lost.
stop_conditions: STOP picking if processing is more than an hour behind: you are manufacturing waste — shift everyone to processing.
STOP if anyone shows heat-illness signs: shade, water, rest — the harvest can wait, heat stroke cannot.
STOP if equipment breaks and no backup exists: do not hand-process a machine's volume — triage what can be saved and compost the rest.
STOP the day if quality is dropping from speed: bruised, dirty product stored badly is worse than less product stored well.

title: Train a new hand with the teach-back method
mechanism_check: New hands get hurt and break things because training is 'watch me once, now do it' — watching is not doing, and doing once is not knowing.
Teach-back works by reversing the flow: the learner explains and demonstrates the task back to the teacher, which exposes the gaps watching hides.
The failure mode is the expert's blind spot: the trainer skips the step they do unconsciously, and the learner invents a wrong version of it.
improvised_tools: A training buddy assignment: every new hand has one named teacher
A short task list for week one: five real jobs, not orientation lectures
The teach-back prompt: 'show me and tell me why'
A no-blame correction rule: mistakes in training are the teacher's miss, not the learner's fault
steps: Teacher demonstrates the task once, narrating every step INCLUDING the safety checks they do without thinking.
Learner does the task while the teacher watches silently — no grabbing the tool, no mid-task corrections unless it is unsafe.
Learner then teaches it back: explains each step and why, while doing it a second time.
Teacher corrects only what the teach-back got wrong — that is the precise gap to close.
Sign off the task on the list only after a clean teach-back; until then, the learner works supervised.
Rotate teachers after week one: different hands teach different tricks, and the learner stops copying one person's bad habits.
stop_conditions: STOP the task immediately if the learner is about to do something unsafe: intervene, explain, restart the teach-back.
STOP assigning solo work before the teach-back sign-off: unsupervised and untrained is how injuries happen.
STOP if the teacher will not let the learner touch the tools: watching for a month trains nothing.
STOP blaming the learner for training gaps: if two learners make the same mistake, the teaching is broken, not the learners.

title: Divide the hated jobs fairly with a rotation the crew trusts
mechanism_check: Every farm has jobs nobody wants: mucking, the late feeding, the cold-morning milking. When they fall on the same person by default, resentment compounds until the crew breaks.
Fairness is not equal hours — it is visible rotation: everyone sees that the bad jobs move, and trust comes from the seeing, not the math.
The failure mode is the invisible default: 'Sarah always does it because she's good at it' is how you lose Sarah.
improvised_tools: A written rotation chart on the barn wall — visible beats verbal
A list of the actual hated jobs, named honestly by the crew
A swap rule: anyone can trade a shift, no questions, no guilt
A monthly 10-minute review: is the rotation still fair?
steps: Ask the crew to name the hated jobs out loud — the list must be theirs, not the boss's guess.
Put the jobs on a rotation chart with names and dates, posted where everyone sees it.
Rotate on a fixed cycle (weekly or per-task-count), not on vibes: the chart decides, not the mood.
Allow free swaps with no justification needed — the swap rule defuses 90 percent of grumbling.
Pair the worst job with a small perk: first pick of the next good job, the warm truck, the good gloves.
Review monthly: if someone has carried a hated job twice in a row through swaps, rebalance by assignment.
stop_conditions: STOP if one person 'volunteers' for every bad job: check whether it is truly voluntary — martyrdom is a warning sign.
STOP if the chart exists but the boss overrides it silently: the rotation is dead the first time it is bypassed without explanation.
STOP if swaps always flow one direction (the same person always takes the bad shift): intervene and reassign.
STOP treating complaints as attitude: a fair rotation absorbs complaints; an unfair one manufactures them.

title: Run the harvest-breakdown drill: who does what when the machine dies
mechanism_check: Equipment breaks at peak load — that is physics, not bad luck — so the breakdown plan has to exist BEFORE the breakdown, when everyone is calm.
A crew without a plan does the same thing five ways: three people diagnose, nobody calls for parts, and the field sits.
The drill works by pre-assigning the three jobs every breakdown needs: diagnose, secure the work in progress, and source the fix.
improvised_tools: A breakdown card taped inside each machine's cab or on the barn wall: who to call, where the manual is, where spares live
Pre-assigned roles: diagnostician, field-securer, parts-runner
A spares kit per machine (see the maintenance rotation, homestead-045)
A backup plan per critical machine: rent, borrow, or hand-finish — decided in advance, not in panic
steps: When a machine dies mid-harvest, the operator stops it safely, shuts it down, and calls the drill — no heroics, no 'one more pass.'
Diagnostician takes the machine: manual out, symptoms listed, the 15-minute rule — if it is not diagnosed in 15 minutes, it is a parts-or-pro call.
Field-securer handles the crop in progress: cover it, move it, or triage what will spoil — the crop does not wait for the repair.
Parts-runner moves: spares kit first, then the call list (dealer, neighbor, rental) — with the exact part name from the manual.
Leader decides at 30 minutes: fix, rent/borrow the backup, or triage the harvest — one decision, announced to all.
Afterward, log the failure on the maintenance chart and restock the spares kit before the next season.
stop_conditions: STOP anyone from working under or inside a machine that is not locked out and blocked: harvest pressure does not suspend physics.
STOP the 15-minute diagnosis from becoming an hour of guessing: escalate to the pro call rather than burning the day.
STOP if the 'fix' involves bypassing a safety interlock: park the machine and execute the backup plan.
STOP repeating a breakdown twice in one season without changing the maintenance plan: the system failed, not the part.
